mcqs.question: What is the biggest scoring mistake candidates make when answering "which pattern fits this scenario"?
options: Naming the specific pattern immediately, without first stating what varies in the scenario
Spending too long clarifying the scenario before naming any pattern at all
Naming the wrong pattern family but the right specific pattern anyway
Using a UML diagram to explain the pattern instead of describing it verbally
mcqs.explanation: The skeleton earns credit at each step — naming what varies, then the family, then the specific pattern. Skipping to the pattern name first, even when it's the right pattern, loses credit for showing you diagnosed the problem before naming the solution. Over-clarifying isn't the failure mode described here, and a diagram is a supplement, not the core skill being tested.

mcqs.question: A checkout needs one call site whose payment behavior swaps between providers at runtime. Which pattern does this describe?
options: Observer — because multiple providers could be notified of the payment
Strategy — because one caller picks a runtime-swappable behavior for the same operation
Factory — because the payment provider needs to be constructed differently each time
Facade — because the checkout is hiding provider-specific complexity behind one call
mcqs.explanation: The clue is one operation whose implementation swaps at runtime — that's Strategy's signature. Observer would fit if independent listeners reacted to a completed payment, not the payment behavior itself. Factory concerns which class gets constructed, not which behavior runs. Facade simplifies an API surface, which isn't what's described here.

mcqs.question: A scenario has exactly two payment types that will never expand, with no requirement to swap at runtime. What's the strongest interview answer?
options: Strategy, because it's always safer to use a named pattern than a plain conditional
Factory, because two types is enough to justify centralizing construction
A plain conditional is enough here — reserve Strategy for when variants grow past a handful or need runtime swapping
Observer, so future variants can be added without touching the checkout class
mcqs.explanation: Recognizing when a scenario is too small for a pattern is part of the skill being tested — two fixed variants with no runtime-swap requirement don't need Strategy's machinery. "Always safer to use a pattern" is exactly the over-engineering instinct this follow-up is probing against; Observer and Factory don't even address this scenario's actual variation.

mcqs.question: A payment flow always runs charge, then email receipt, then update inventory, in that fixed order, with no pluggable listeners. Why is Observer the wrong pattern here?
options: Observer requires the subject to know exactly which listeners exist ahead of time
Observer only works with a single fixed sequence of steps, never multiple listeners
Observer is only valid for GUI event handling, not backend workflows
Observer's value is a subject not needing to know how many independent, pluggable listeners react — a fixed, ordered pipeline is a different shape entirely
mcqs.explanation: Observer's whole point is decoupling a subject from an unknown, independent set of reactors. A fixed three-step pipeline with no independent listeners is better modeled as a plain sequence or Template Method. Observer works fine outside GUIs, and it doesn't require knowing listeners ahead of time — quite the opposite.
